title: Why Japanese Doctors Still Prescribe Antibiotics for the Common Cold
hook: Japanese clinics have long handed out antibiotics for colds that don't need them — yet the country's resistance numbers don't look like a cautionary tale. Here's the mechanism behind both halves of that puzzle.
target_query: why do japanese doctors prescribe antibiotics for colds
free_section_html:
Japanese doctors prescribe antibiotics for the common cold, or kaze, more often than clinical guidelines recommend because the country's fee-for-service payment system, short consultation times, and patient expectations all push in the same direction — toward writing a prescription rather than sending a patient home empty-handed. Surveys of outpatient visits for upper respiratory infections conducted before Japan's 2016 national response found that a majority of these visits, most of them for viral illnesses that antibiotics cannot touch, still ended with an antibiotic in hand.

The drug of choice mattered as much as the decision to prescribe. Clinics have historically favored oral third-generation cephalosporins and macrolides — broad-spectrum drugs meant for more serious infections — over narrow-spectrum penicillins that are cheaper, more targeted, and, for most bacterial throat and ear infections, just as effective. This is close to the reverse of what antibiotic stewardship programs elsewhere try to achieve, where narrow-spectrum drugs are the default and broad-spectrum ones are reserved for confirmed or severe cases.

The average consultation for a cold in Japan runs only a few minutes. In that window, a doctor weighing whether to disappoint a patient who came in expecting medicine, or to spend time explaining why a virus doesn't respond to antibiotics, often takes the faster path. Clinics that dispense drugs on-site have also had a direct financial stake in writing prescriptions, since dispensing generates its own fee under the national insurance point system.

In 2016, Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare launched a national action plan explicitly targeting this pattern, aiming to cut oral antibiotic use by roughly a third within five years and to sharply reduce prescriptions for children's colds and sore throats. Consumption did fall, though not all the way to target, and the mix of drugs shifted only slowly. The more interesting question is what happens next: why a country with this prescribing habit hasn't seen the resistance crisis the numbers alone would predict, and where the strategy goes from here.
paid_body_html:
The prescribing habits described above would, on paper, predict a country in the middle of a resistance emergency. Broad-spectrum drugs handed out for viral illnesses are supposed to be exactly the recipe that breeds resistant bacteria. Japan's actual position among wealthy nations is more ambiguous than that — better in some respects, worse in others, and shaped by structural features of its health system that rarely make it into the headline statistics.

The reimbursement math behind the prescription pad

Japan's universal health insurance system pays clinics and hospitals through a national fee schedule, known as tensuu, a point system in which nearly every act — a consultation, a test, a dispensed drug — carries a fixed price set by the government and revised every two years. For much of the postwar period, clinics that dispensed medicine directly from an in-house pharmacy earned a dispensing fee on top of the consultation fee, giving physicians a direct financial interest in writing a prescription rather than sending a patient to an outside pharmacy with nothing more than advice to rest and drink fluids.

A policy called ishi-yaku bungyo, the separation of prescribing and dispensing, has pushed hard against this since the 1990s, encouraging patients to fill prescriptions at independent pharmacies rather than at the clinic counter. The separation is now close to universal in cities, but it did not remove the underlying habit of reaching for a prescription pad as the default conclusion to a visit — it only moved where the pills get counted out.

"Please give me something strong": the unwritten bargain

Japanese primary care carries an informal expectation, familiar to anyone who has sat in a crowded clinic waiting room during flu season, that a doctor's visit should end with medicine. Patients have sometimes asked directly for a stronger drug, associating strength with effectiveness rather than with the narrower question of whether the drug matches the pathogen. Physicians managing a full afternoon of patients, often with visits budgeted at a few minutes each, have had little room to negotiate that expectation with an explanation of viral versus bacterial illness. Writing the prescription that satisfies the immediate encounter has been, in a narrow sense, the path of least resistance for the doctor even as it works against resistance in the broader sense.

This dynamic explains why the drugs chosen were often the wrong tool for the job in a second way. Oral third-generation cephalosporins, a class widely prescribed for colds and sore throats in Japan, are poorly absorbed by the digestive tract compared with older, narrower-spectrum antibiotics. A patient could be simultaneously overtreated — receiving a drug with no business fighting a viral infection — and undertreated, in the rare case of an actual bacterial infection, because too little of the active drug reached the bloodstream. Japanese infectious disease specialists have flagged this specific mismatch, between broad-spectrum intent and weak pharmacological delivery, as one of the more perverse features of the country's outpatient prescribing pattern.

What the 2016 national plan changed, and what it didn't

The National Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, adopted by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare in 2016, set explicit numeric targets for the first time: a substantial cut in oral antimicrobial consumption per person, a much larger reduction in prescriptions for children with colds and middle-ear infections, and a smaller reduction in the use of injectable antibiotics, over roughly five years. The plan paired these targets with clinical guidelines for common infections, continuing medical education campaigns aimed at physicians, and public information campaigns aimed at patients, explicitly trying to unwind the expectation that a cold visit should end in a prescription.

National surveillance data tracked through the Japan Nosocomial Infections Surveillance network, known as JANIS, and through pharmaceutical sales data, showed consumption falling over the plan period, though not reaching every target, and progress was uneven across drug classes — narrow-spectrum penicillin use grew only modestly even as some broad-spectrum categories declined. A successor plan covering the years through 2027 has continued the same targets with revised numbers, an acknowledgment that the first five years narrowed the problem without solving it.

The resistance paradox

Despite this prescribing history, Japan has not tracked with the countries that show the highest rates of resistant infection among wealthy nations. Rates of certain resistant organisms tracked through JANIS, including drug-resistant strains found in hospital settings, have in some categories held roughly flat or improved over the past decade, even as outpatient antibiotic use for colds remained a persistent problem through the mid-2010s. Researchers who study this gap point to several contributing factors rather than a single explanation: comparatively strict infection control practices inside Japanese hospitals, a health system that catches and isolates outbreaks early through mandatory reporting requirements, and a culture of hand hygiene and mask use in clinical settings that predates the pandemic by decades and limits the spread of resistant organisms once they emerge.

None of this means Japan's antibiotic prescribing habits are harmless. Resistance is a population-level and, increasingly, a global problem — a resistant organism that develops in one country's outpatient clinics does not stay within that country's hospitals, and antibiotic use in Japanese livestock and companion animals adds a separate pressure that is not captured by outpatient prescribing data at all. The honest picture is a mixed one: a prescribing culture that genuinely needs to change, sitting inside a broader system of infection control and surveillance that has, so far, kept the worst consequences from showing up as clearly as the prescribing numbers alone would suggest they should.

What comes next

The current national plan leans more heavily on primary care education than its predecessor, training general practitioners to explain the difference between viral and bacterial illness in the few minutes a visit allows, and on point-of-care testing that can tell a clinician within minutes whether a sore throat is bacterial before a prescription gets written at all. Whether that closes the gap between Japan's prescribing habits and its resistance numbers, or whether the surveillance advantages that have cushioned the country so far start to erode, is a question the next five years of JANIS data will answer more clearly than any single policy announcement can.
key_takeaways: Japan's fee-for-service point system historically rewarded clinics for dispensing drugs on-site, giving doctors a direct financial stake in writing prescriptions for colds.
Before 2016, most outpatient visits for upper respiratory infections in Japan ended with an antibiotic, despite most colds being viral and unresponsive to antibiotics.
Japanese clinics have favored broad-spectrum oral third-generation cephalosporins, which are also poorly absorbed by the body, over cheaper, more targeted narrow-spectrum penicillins.
A 2016 national action plan set numeric targets to cut oral antibiotic use and pediatric prescribing; consumption fell but not to every target, prompting a successor plan through 2027.
Despite high outpatient prescribing, Japan has avoided the worst resistance outcomes seen elsewhere, likely due to strict hospital infection control and the JANIS national surveillance network.
meta_title: Why Do Japanese Doctors Prescribe Antibiotics for Colds?
